advances: Selective deletion of fourth sites admits an original-normalizer comparison with the actual selective target occupancy exponential moment and the absolute constant 64. The anchor pool need only be eligible for the coordinates being deleted; cheaper four-site coordinates remain in the core. The comparison gives an explicit retained original mass and composes directly with the accepted residual-core/three-site transport, without requiring core certificates at every residual cutoff. Obtaining an absolute bound on this occupancy exponential moment remains a separate mathematical task.

The original weighted exchange setup from declared accepted facts `9f6ebd76c13f58a8` and `a2136c3725dae630` is proved here in normalized-kernel form with its changed counts explicitly mapped. Declared accepted facts `8668ed0d436b9cba` and `6fe9007fe1ba4c4b` supply only the original residual-core/three-site moment transport with the exact support, parameter, normalizer, and ambient-halfspace maps in (6)-(8) and the proof. All selective deletion counts, target overlaps, and the exponential-moment comparison are proved above.
proof:
All normalizers are positive because the zero spatial vector contributes its height-zero atom. The complete height tails satisfy \(f_E\le f_{E'}\) whenever \(E'\le E\). We prove a finite source-to-target comparison using these actual tails. This is the weighted exchange principle of `9f6ebd76c13f58a8`, as used in `a2136c3725dae630`, with normalized outgoing edges so their possible target overlaps can be summed pointwise.

Restrict sources and targets to feasible vectors, those of energy at most \(T\). Construct a nonnegative kernel \(K(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\) from full feasible sources to selective feasible targets, with every row summing to 1 and every positive entry satisfying \(\Gamma(\mathbf y)\le\Gamma(\mathbf x)\). Define its column load \(L(\mathbf y)=\sum_{\mathbf x}K(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\). Monotonicity of the complete tails then gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
Z_{\rm full}
&=\sum_{\mathbf x,\mathbf y}f_{\Gamma(\mathbf x)}K(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\\
&\le\sum_{\mathbf x,\mathbf y}f_{\Gamma(\mathbf y)}K(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)
=\sum_{\mathbf y}f_{\Gamma(\mathbf y)}L(\mathbf y).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
$$
The following construction proves \(L(\mathbf y)\le e^{64F_{P,J}(\mathbf y)}\). Each source is assigned to exactly one case. A source with no three in \(J\) is already selective and maps to itself with kernel entry 1. Thus these sources contribute exactly 1 to every feasible target's column load. Every remaining source has \(\ell=|\lbrace i\in J:x_i=3\rbrace|\ge1\). All unmentioned coordinates are left unchanged in every case, including retained pool threes and binary companions.

First consider sources with \(Q_{P,J}(\mathbf x)\ge m/32\). Clip their threes in \(J\) to twos and give the resulting single target kernel entry 1. This lowers energy, since \(C_{4,i}\ge B_i\), and preserves \(Q_{P,J}\). Fix a target \(\mathbf y\), and abbreviate \(q=Q_{P,J}(\mathbf y)\). A preimage is specified by a nonempty subset of its two-coordinates in \(J\), those which were threes. Therefore the load from this case is zero for \(q<m/32\), and otherwise at most \(2^q-1\). Since \(\log2<3/4\), for \(q\ge m/32\) one has \(q\log2\le24q^2/m\le24F_{P,J}(\mathbf y)\). In all cases the clipping contribution obeys
$$
L_{\rm clip}(\mathbf y)\le e^{24F_{P,J}(\mathbf y)}-1.
\tag{10}
$$
For example, the elementary inequality \(e^{3/4}>1+3/4+(3/4)^2/2>2\) verifies the numerical logarithm bound used here.

Now consider sources with \(q_{\rm src}=Q_{P,J}(\mathbf x)<m/32\) and \(a=A_P(\mathbf x)\ge m/4\). Their \(\ell\) threes in \(J\) satisfy \(\ell\le q_{\rm src}<m/32\). For each \(\ell\)-element subset of the \(a\) pool one-coordinates, clip all threes in \(J\) to twos and change the selected pool ones to twos. Give each of these distinct targets kernel entry \(1/\binom a\ell\). The energy change is at most
$$
\ell(b-1)-\sum_{i\in J:x_i=3}(C_{4,i}-B_i)
\le\ell(b-1)-\sum_{i\in J:x_i=3}(B_i-1)\le0.
\tag{11}
$$
Consequently all targets are feasible and each source row sums to 1.

For a fixed target \(\mathbf y\) with \(q=Q_{P,J}(\mathbf y)\), an inverse source with the indicated \(\ell\) is specified by an \(\ell\)-subset of target twos in \(J\) to change back to threes, and an \(\ell\)-subset of target twos in \(P\) to change back to ones. These two subsets determine the source uniquely. There is no matching factor. Each available set has size at most \(q\), so the number of inverse sources is at most \(q^{2\ell}/(\ell!)^2\). On any such edge the source pool one-count is \(a=A_P(\mathbf y)+\ell\), and
$$
\binom a\ell\ge\frac{(a-\ell+1)^\ell}{\ell!}
\ge\frac{(m/8)^\ell}{\ell!},
\tag{12}
$$
because \(a\ge m/4\) and \(\ell<m/32\). Dividing the inverse count by this lower outdegree and summing over all \(\ell\ge1\), allowing extra nonnegative terms, proves
$$
L_{\rm one}(\mathbf y)
\le\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{(8q^2/m)^\ell}{\ell!}
\le e^{8F_{P,J}(\mathbf y)}-1.
\tag{13}
$$
Here \(Q_{P,J}(\mathbf y)=q_{\rm src}+\ell\), since precisely the selected pool ones are newly counted as occupied; this count relation is consistent with all inverse choices above. No global count of high-cost coordinates has been substituted.

It remains to handle sources with \(q_{\rm src}=Q_{P,J}(\mathbf x)<m/32\) and \(a=A_P(\mathbf x)<m/4\). Since they have \(\ell\ge1\) threes in \(J\), \(1\le\ell\le q_{\rm src}\). Put
$$
h=\min\left\lbrace b-1,\left\lfloor\frac{m}{8q_{\rm src}}\right\rfloor\right\rbrace,
\qquad z=|\lbrace i\in P:x_i=0\rbrace|.
\tag{14}
$$
The integer \(h\) is positive. At most \(q_{\rm src}\) pool coordinates lie in \(\lbrace2,3\rbrace\), so
$$
z>\frac{23m}{32},\qquad h\ell\le\frac m8.
\tag{15}
$$
For each \(h\ell\)-subset of the pool zero-coordinates, clip the threes in \(J\) to twos and change the selected zeros to ones. Give these distinct targets kernel entry \(1/\binom z{h\ell}\). Their energy change is at most
$$
h\ell-\sum_{i\in J:x_i=3}(C_{4,i}-B_i)
\le h\ell-\ell(b-1)\le0.
\tag{16}
$$
The subset choices exist by (15), and their normalized row sums are 1. This transformation preserves \(Q_{P,J}\). Thus for a target with \(q=Q_{P,J}(\mathbf y)\), every inverse source in this case has \(q_{\rm src}=q\), so the same \(h=\min\lbrace b-1,\lfloor m/(8q)\rfloor\rbrace\) is fixed by the target. Such a target necessarily has \(1\le q<m/32\).

Write \(A=A_P(\mathbf y)\) and \(z_{\rm tar}=|\lbrace i\in P:y_i=0\rbrace|\). For any inverse source with fixed \(\ell\), one has \(A=a+h\ell\) and \(z=z_{\rm tar}+h\ell\). In particular the denominator of its kernel entry is fixed by the target and \(\ell\). The inverse choices are an \(\ell\)-subset of target twos in \(J\), and an \(h\ell\)-subset of target pool ones, to restore respectively to threes and zeros. They specify every source coordinate, with no pairing factor. Hence the total load for this fixed \(\ell\) is at most
$$
\binom q\ell\frac{\binom A{h\ell}}{\binom z{h\ell}}.
\tag{17}
$$
This conclusion also follows by partitioning sources by their counts, but no disjointness of different \(\ell\)-target sets is assumed. Invalid inverse choices only decrease the load.

For any nonempty inverse class, (15) and \(a<m/4\) give \(A<3m/8\) and \(z_{\rm tar}>19m/32\). Put \(\theta=A/(z_{\rm tar}+1)\). The product formula and these bounds yield
$$
\frac{\binom A{h\ell}}{\binom z{h\ell}}
=\prod_{j=0}^{h\ell-1}\frac{A-j}{z-j}
\le\theta^{h\ell},
\qquad
\theta\le\frac23,
\qquad
\theta\le\frac{2A}{m}.
\tag{18}
$$
We claim
$$
\theta^h\le\frac{32(q+A/b)}m.
\tag{19}
$$
If \(h=b-1\), the two bounds on \(\theta\) give
$$
\theta^h\le\frac{2A}{m}\left(\frac23\right)^{b-2}
\le\frac{4A}{bm}.
\tag{20}
$$
For the last inequality, \(b(2/3)^{b-2}\le2\) for every integer \(b\ge2\): it equals 2 at \(b=2\), and the ratio of successive values is \(2(b+1)/(3b)\le1\). If instead \(h=\lfloor m/(8q)\rfloor\), then \(q<m/32\) implies \(m/(8q)>4\) and \(h\ge m/(16q)\). Bernoulli's inequality gives \( (3/2)^h\ge1+h/2\ge h/2\), and hence
$$
\theta^h\le(2/3)^h\le2/h\le32q/m.
\tag{21}
$$
At least one of these two cases applies, including equality between the entries defining \(h\). Each proves (19).

Combining (17)-(19), and using \(\binom q\ell\le q^\ell/\ell!\), bounds the fixed-\(\ell\) load by \( (32F_{P,J}(\mathbf y))^\ell/\ell!\). The target itself fixes \(q,h,A,z_{\rm tar}\); there is therefore no extra multiplicity from different source count classes. Summing over \(\ell\ge1\) proves, also for targets with no such inverse sources,
$$
L_{\rm zero}(\mathbf y)\le e^{32F_{P,J}(\mathbf y)}-1.
\tag{22}
$$

Every full feasible source occurs exactly once among the selective identity sources, large-occupancy clipping sources, small-occupancy high-pool-one sources, and small-occupancy low-pool-one sources. The target sets of these cases may overlap. The column load is their sum, so (10), (13), and (22) give, with \(F=F_{P,J}(\mathbf y)\ge0\),
$$
\begin{aligned}
L(\mathbf y)
&\le1+(e^{24F}-1)+(e^{8F}-1)+(e^{32F}-1)\\
&\le e^{24F}e^{8F}e^{32F}=e^{64F}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{23}
$$
The second inequality follows by writing each exponential as (1) plus a nonnegative number and expanding their product. In particular it explicitly pays for all overlaps, including clipping targets also reached by small-source exchanges. The row normalization in (9) prevents duplication of source mass. Substituting (23) into (9), and adding the zero-weight infeasible targets if desired, proves (3).

For (5), let \(\delta=Z_{\rm sel}/Z_{\rm full}\). The supports in (4) satisfy \(\mathcal A_{\rm sel}\subseteq\mathcal A_{\rm full}\), and \(p^{\rm full}_{\mathbf z}=\delta p^{\rm sel}_{\mathbf z}\) at every selective atom. For every closed ambient halfspace \(H\), \(p^{\rm full}(H)\ge\delta p^{\rm sel}(H)\). Taking infima over the same halfspaces containing any selective atom yields \(\tau_{p^{\rm full}}(\mathbf z)\ge\delta\tau_{p^{\rm sel}}(\mathbf z)\). Restricting the sampling sum to selective atoms gives
$$
M_3(p^{\rm full})\ge\delta^4M_3(p^{\rm sel})
\ge\mathcal B_{P,J}^{-4}M_3(p^{\rm sel}),
\tag{24}
$$
where the last inequality is (3). The four powers are one sampling factor and three depth factors, all using the full original law on the left.

For the direct transport, the zero core vector has energy zero, so all normalizers in (6) are positive. Reordering coordinates as core, tail \(J\), and height is a coordinate permutation and preserves the ambient family of closed affine halfspaces. The selective support and law then agree exactly with (2) of accepted `8668ed0d436b9cba`, with the parameter and normalization map given after (6). The identity for \(\pi\) follows by the exact substitution \(t=t'+\Gamma_J(\mathbf u)\), retaining the endpoints \(h_{\rm core}(\mathbf x)\le t'\le T-\Gamma_J(\mathbf u)\). That predecessor's fourth-root transport, followed by (24), is exactly (7). Restricting its nonnegative sum to residual cutoffs in \(\mathcal G\) and taking fourth powers proves (8), since \(r+s+1=N\). For the all-cutoff specialization, choose \(\mathcal G=\lbrace T-\Gamma_J(\mathbf u):\mathbf u\in\lbrace0,1,2\rbrace^J,\ \Gamma_J(\mathbf u)\le T\rbrace\). Under its stated hypothesis the core bound holds for every \(U\in\mathcal G\), so (8) applies to this choice. Every feasible tail vector has its residual cutoff in this \(\mathcal G\); hence the defining sum for \(\alpha_{\mathcal G}\) includes all entries of the probability law \(\pi\) and equals 1. Accepted `6fe9007fe1ba4c4b` also applies with the same \(r,s,T,\beta,D_{\rm core},h_{\rm core},q_{\mathbf x}=1,\Gamma_J,Z_{\rm sel}\), and \(p^{\rm sel}\), giving that same specialization. This assertion concerns the displayed all-cutoff choice of \(\mathcal G\), while the arbitrary-set conclusion (8) retains its actual \(\alpha_{\mathcal G}\).

If \(J\) is empty, only identity sources exist and \(Z_{\rm full}=Z_{\rm sel}\); the inequalities still hold, and the direct transport uses its allowed \(s=0\) case. If \(T=0\), both laws consist only of the zero spatial vector at height zero, with \(F=0\) and \(\mathcal B_{P,J}=1\). For \(q=0\), no nonidentity source can reach the target in any construction, so its column load is exactly 1 and no division by \(q\) is made. If \(m\le32\), there is no nonidentity source in a small-occupancy case, and the clipping estimate alone suffices. All energy comparisons, feasibility restrictions, height endpoints, and halfspace containments are weak. Equal costs, equality \(C_{4,i}=2B_i-1\), and \(\beta=0\) are included. Thus no original height atom or support or halfspace boundary has been discarded.
